n: In this lecture we shall consider the bioethical issues of transplantology. Organ transplantation involves medical factors, namely immunological matching, the recipient's health and immunosuppressive therapy, as well as ethical and legal questions. The greatest difficulties are associated with ethical and legal problems: the confirmation of death, the retrieval of the organ, its allocation and commercialisation. Donor organs are in serious shortage worldwide: even in the USA and Europe about 35 per cent of those in need do not live to receive a transplant. The aim of the class is to analyse the types of transplantation, donation models, the criterion of death and international documents from a bioethical standpoint.

Let us become familiar with the outline of the lecture. First, the types of transplantation and donation will be considered, then the criterion of human death. Next, the models of consent, the organ shortage, and the problems of allocation and trafficking will be covered. Finally, the views of religions, international documents and the procedure in Uzbekistan, according to Mukhamedova (2021), will be covered. The sequence is as follows: types and donation, the brain death criterion, consent models, shortage, allocation and trafficking, and finally religion and international documents.

What is transplantation? Transplantation is the transfer of an organ or tissue from one organism to another. It is usually divided into experimental and clinical transplantation. The experimental stage is regarded as preclinical; biological, surgical and organisational issues are resolved at this stage. At the experimental stage, the state of the recipient's immune system and the question of new drugs are studied.

Let us consider the tasks of experimental transplantation. Experimental transplantation is the stage that precedes clinical transplantation. At this stage the biological, surgical and organisational problems of transplanting organs and tissues are worked out. One of the important problems is the state of the recipient's immune system after a donor organ has been transplanted. It can be partly solved through experiment. New drugs that help genetically different organs and tissues to be accepted are also developed at this stage.

The types of transplantation differ according to who the donor is: the recipient himself, a twin, another person or an animal. Accordingly, there are four types. In autotransplantation the donor is the recipient himself. In isotransplantation the donor is an identical twin. In allotransplantation the donor is a genetically different person. In xenotransplantation the donor is an animal of another biological species. Allotransplantation is also called homotransplantation, and xenotransplantation is also called interspecies transplantation. Attention: iso and allo are not the same thing. In isotransplantation the donor is a twin who is genetically completely identical to the recipient.

Now let us look at auto- and isotransplantation. In autotransplantation, that is, autologous transplantation, the recipient himself is the donor of the graft. In severe burns, skin from an undamaged area is transplanted to the burned area. In leukaemia, lymphoma and chemosensitive malignant tumours, bone marrow or haematopoietic stem cells are autotransplanted after high-dose chemotherapy. In isotransplantation, by contrast, the donor is an identical twin who is immunologically and genetically completely identical to the recipient.

One must know the difference between allo- and xenotransplantation precisely. In allotransplantation the donor is another person, genetically and immunologically different; its other name is homotransplantation. In xenotransplantation the organ is taken from an animal of another biological species, which is why it is called interspecies. Attention: allo means from human to human, xeno means from animal to human, and they differ. Do not confuse the two.

The use of transplantation technologies has certain limitations, both medical and ethical-legal. Medical factors include the immunological matching of the donor, the recipient's health and immunosuppressive therapy. Ethical-legal factors are the confirmation of the fact of death, the retrieval of the organ from the body, allocation and commercialisation. The greatest difficulties are related not to medical but to ethical and legal problems. Commercialisation means subordinating transplantological activity to the aim of making a profit.

t: Case analysis 1: identifying the type of transplantation
n: The first case analysis is devoted to identifying the type of transplantation. Situation A: a patient with a severe burn was given skin from his own undamaged area. What type is this? Situation B: a patient with leukaemia was given his own bone marrow or haematopoietic stem cells after high-dose chemotherapy. Situation C: the donor is an identical twin, immunologically and genetically completely identical to the recipient. What type is this? Question: to which of the types — auto-, iso-, allo- or xenotransplantation — would you assign A, B and C, and why?

In the case of a living donor, a harm-benefit dilemma arises. Retrieving an organ from a living donor harms his health, so the principle of non-maleficence is violated. The physician faces the dilemma of harm to the donor's health versus saving the recipient's life. The chain is as follows: an organ is retrieved from the donor, there is a risk of harm to the donor, the recipient's life is saved, and benefit and harm are weighed against each other. The rule: the dilemma is resolved by weighing benefit against harm, and the benefit obtained must exceed the harm.

t: Circle of living donors and cadaveric donation
n: The circle of living donors is defined by law in different countries. Close relatives include a twin, brothers, sisters and parents. Non-relatives include a relative of the spouse, a friend or a close acquaintance. The circle is determined by the law of each country. Retrieving organs from a cadaver is the most widespread type of donation. Its three main problems are the confirmation of death, the voluntary expression of consent and the attitude of religion.

The first quick question. First question: which type of transplantation is it in which the recipient himself is the donor? Answer: autotransplantation, that is, autologous transplantation. Second question: by which rule is the living donor dilemma resolved? The benefit obtained must exceed the harm inflicted. Third question: name the three problems of cadaveric donation. Answer: confirmation of death, the wish to refuse voluntarily, and the permission of religion.

t: History of the concept of death: timeline
n: Now let us turn to the history of the concept of death. At the end of the twentieth century, owing to the development of resuscitation and transplantology, determining the moment of death became a bioethical problem. The main question: which state of the organism is recognised as the moment of death? The concept of brain death was developed after the French neurologists Mollaret and Goulon described the "coma dépassé". In 1968 the Harvard criteria of brain death were created. In the same year the world medical community adopted the Declaration of Sydney. In the following years laws were adopted in many countries.

Let us dwell on the criterion and essence of brain death. In the present understanding, brain death is irreversible coma, cessation of spontaneous breathing and loss of all brainstem reflexes. In this state the whole brain perishes together with the brainstem. Death is the failure of the delicate systems of the organism; they cannot be replaced by artificial systems. The human brain is precisely such a system. Attention: coma alone is not brain death. In the criterion, irreversible coma, cessation of breathing and absence of brainstem reflexes occur together; in most countries this is the main criterion.

t: Case analysis 2: determining the time of death
n: The second case analysis concerns determining the time of death. Situation: the patient is in irreversible coma, does not breathe spontaneously, and has no brainstem reflexes. Breathing and circulation are maintained by a machine. Question: by which sign is the time of death recognised in this state — by cardiac activity maintained by the machine, or by the state of the brain? Direction of the answer: in most countries brain death is the main criterion of human death, and death is confirmed by this criterion. Addition: the Islamic Fiqh Academy (1988) permitted transplantation from a person with brain death whose breathing and circulation are maintained artificially.

t: Three models of organ retrieval from a cadaver
n: Three main models of organ retrieval from a cadaver are in operation: the old procedure, presumed consent and presumed dissent. Under the old procedure, after death the body is regarded as the property of the state, and the state uses the organs for scientific purposes. Under presumed consent, it is assumed that consent has been given in advance, and if there is no objection, the organ is retrieved. Under presumed dissent, it is assumed that dissent exists in advance, and if consent has been formalised, the organ is retrieved. In the modern world, organ retrieval is carried out according to the principles of presumed consent or presumed dissent.

Let us consider presumed consent. A presumption is the recognition that a person has given consent in advance. A person who does not agree must state his objection in the established manner. The procedure is as follows: the person dies, and it is checked whether dissent has been declared. If not, there is a right to retrieve the organ. If so, the organ cannot be retrieved. If the person, his relatives or his legal representative have submitted an objection to the institution, the organ is not retrieved.

t: Presumed dissent and the donor card
n: Under presumed dissent, a person is considered to be in disagreement in advance. If he agrees, he must formalise this in the established manner. In some countries, the document of consent to organ retrieval is formalised during the person's lifetime. In the USA, the legal form of this is the "donor card". In the USA, Germany, Canada, France and Italy, "requested consent" is in force: without formal consent no organ is retrieved. Attention: presumed consent differs from presumed dissent. In the former an objection is declared; in the latter, consent is given.

In the practice of states there are two approaches. In Austria, Belgium, Spain, Hungary and the Czech Republic, legal norms are adapted to presumed consent: consent is assumed to exist in advance, and those who do not agree declare their objection. In the USA, Germany, Canada, France and Italy, on the other hand, presumed dissent, that is, "requested consent", is in force: a person who agrees formalises his consent, and without formal consent organ retrieval is impossible. In about 40 countries the transplantation programme is regulated by a section of the Constitution or by a special law.

The third case analysis concerns applying the presumption. Situation: a person has died. Neither he during his lifetime nor his relatives have submitted an objection to the healthcare institution; there is no formal document of consent. Under presumed consent, if the deceased or his relatives have not objected, the right to retrieve organs and tissues is granted. Under presumed dissent, if there is no legally formalised consent, the use of organs and tissues is not permitted. Question: in which model is organ retrieval possible? Attention: the action required differs between these two presumptions.

t: Donor organ shortage and ways of solving it
n: On the shortage of donor organs and ways of solving it. Even in the USA and Europe, about 35 per cent of those in need do not receive a transplant. One solution is to call for voluntary donation of organs on the basis of consent formalised during one's lifetime. Artificial organs, cell culture and animal organs are also being developed as a solution. There is also the route of obtaining tissue from stem cells. Thus, a solution to the shortage is being sought in several directions.

Now artificial organs and therapeutic cloning. The artificial kidney machine is widely used; artificial heart valves, joints and the lens of the eye are also in use. However, artificial organs require great expense and testing. In therapeutic cloning, tissue is grown from a somatic cell; the person becomes both donor and recipient. From the ethical standpoint, opening up a donor is not required, and immunological compatibility may be resolved. Attention: cloning is still at the research stage, and experiments on cartilage and muscle are far from introduction into practice; artificial organs, however, are used in practice.

Let us consider the advantages and risks of xenotransplantation. The chromosomes and organ structure of the pig are close to those of humans, it multiplies quickly, and it is a domestic animal. A human gene is introduced into a transgenic pig, so that the likelihood of rejection is reduced. The greatest dangers are the transmission of infections and viruses, and the compatibility of the animal organ with the human organism. Animal protection campaigners and representatives of transhumanism are opposed; there is also a psychological and ethical problem for the individual.

The second quick question. First question: what are the five ways of solving the shortage? Answer: voluntary donation, an artificial organ, bioelectronics and nanotechnology, cell culture, animal donors. Second question: why was the pig chosen for xenotransplantation? Its chromosomes and organ structure are close to those of humans, it multiplies quickly, and it is a domestic animal. Third question: what are the greatest scientific and medical risks of xenotransplantation? The transmission of infection and viruses, and the problem of organ compatibility. Fourth question: why is therapeutic cloning ethically favourable? There is no need to open up the donor surgically; the starting material is the person's own somatic cells.

t: Organ allocation: justice and waiting lists
n: Organ allocation is topical all over the world. It is part of the problem of the shortage of donor organs and rests on the principle of justice. Allocation is carried out through "waiting lists". They record the features of the patient's health. The process is as follows: the patient is entered on the waiting list, the state of his health is recorded, a donor organ becomes available, and immunological compatibility is checked. Even if the sickest patient stands first on the list, he may not reach the operation if he is immunologically incompatible; if there is no match, the turn does not pass.

Commercialisation is the subordination of transplantology to the aim of making a profit. The scarcer organs are, the more they are turning into a scarce and very expensive commodity. In many countries the buying and selling of organs is prohibited by law. Nevertheless, according to the law that "demand creates supply", a "black market" exists. Usually one of a pair of organs is sold, the best known being the kidney. Commercialisation is assessed as contrary to the lofty humanistic idea of transplantology.

Let us consider the international documents against organ trafficking. The World Medical Association rejects the sale and purchase of organs and calls on governments to prevent their use for commercial purposes. The World Health Assembly in 1987 expressed concern about organ trafficking; by resolution WHA44.25 (1991) the first World Health Organization guidelines were approved. On 21 May 2010, resolution WHA63.22 approved an updated version of the guidelines. The Declaration of Istanbul (2008) was adopted against transplant tourism and illegal trade; its new version was presented in Madrid in July 2018.

The fourth case analysis concerns the seller-donor. Situation: a person, mainly because of financial need, decided to sell one of his paired organs, his kidney. In many countries such buying and selling is prohibited by law, but a "black market" exists all the same. Retrieving an organ from a living donor harms his health. Therefore the principle of non-maleficence is violated, while the benefit must exceed the harm. Question: which ethical principles are violated in this situation? Answer from the standpoint of the principles of informed voluntary consent and social justice.

t: Harm of organ trafficking and preventive measures
n: On the harm of organ trafficking and measures to prevent it. Firstly, turning the body into a commodity depersonalises the person and causes him moral harm. Secondly, organ trafficking strengthens social injustice: a rich person survives at the expense of the poor. There are three measures. Society must effectively monitor the prohibition of commercialisation and improve funding. A national system for procuring and allocating cadaveric organs must be established. In addition, social protection should be strengthened.

Now religion and transplantology, first of all Christianity. The Russian Orthodox Church holds that organs cannot be an object of buying and selling. Living donation must be based only on voluntary self-sacrifice. The donor must know the expected consequences of organ retrieval. Explantation, that is, organ retrieval, that directly endangers life is morally inadmissible. The Orthodox Church regards presumed consent, that is, treating a person as consenting if no dissent is declared, as an impermissible violation of human freedom. The Catholic Church regards donation as mercy and a moral duty. Protestant theologians consider the sale of organs immoral.

t: Views of religions: Judaism, Buddhism, Christianity
n: Let us compare the views of religions. In Judaism, when it concerns saving a human life, organ transplantation is considered permissible; provided that the deceased gave permission and the family does not object, with special attention to the integrity of the body. In Buddhism, transplantation is envisaged only from a living donor and only if it is a gift to the patient. The Catholic Church regards donation as mercy and a moral duty, but only on a voluntary basis. Attention: Protestants accept organ retrieval, but consider the sale of organs immoral.

On Islam and transplantation. In 1988 the Council of the Islamic Fiqh Academy at its 4th session adopted resolution No. 26 (1/4). If the donor or his relatives agree, retrieval from a cadaver is permissible; if the person is unknown, the head of the Muslims gives consent. In the Sharia, presumed dissent is established; the operation takes place under the supervision of a competent institution. The main provisions of the resolution: the benefit should clearly outweigh the harm; retrieving vital organs from a living person is prohibited; with artificial respiration and circulation in a state of brain death, transplantation is permissible; and trade in organs is categorically prohibited.

t: Case analysis 5: religious and ethical standpoint
n: The fifth case analysis covers the religious and ethical standpoint. Situation: the deceased had agreed during his lifetime to become a donor, but his family is against organ retrieval. How do religions regard this? Question: whose voice is decisive? In Judaism, organ retrieval is possible only if the person permitted it before death and the family does not object. On the question of saving life, permission is given. In Islam, transplantation is possible if the donor during his lifetime or his relatives after death have given consent. Transplantation on a commercial basis is categorically forbidden. The Catholic Church calls donation mercy and a moral duty, but only on a voluntary basis. The Russian Orthodox Church regards presumed consent as a violation of freedom.

Now international declarations. The World Medical Association, that is, the WMA, adopted a declaration on organ transplantation in 1987. The main principle: in any situation the physician is first of all concerned with the health of the person. The chronology of the documents is as follows: Harvard criteria 1968, Declaration of Sydney 1968, WMA declaration 1987, Islamic Academy resolution 1988. Attention: 1968 is the brain death criteria, 1987 is the transplantation declaration. Do not confuse the years.

t: National laws, the genome and UNESCO
n: On national laws, the genome and UNESCO. In about 40 countries of the world, the national transplantation programme is regulated by a section of the Constitution or by a special law; it relies on international norms. In Austria, Belgium, Spain, Hungary and the Czech Republic, presumed consent is in force. In the USA, Germany, Canada, France and Italy, requested consent. According to Article 1 of the Declaration on the Human Genome, the genome is the "heritage of humanity". The International Bioethics Committee proposed a mechanism for the fair distribution of income. UNESCO, that is, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, recognised the ethics of science and technology as one of the priority areas of its strategy for 2002–2007.

Now let us look at the situation in Uzbekistan. In Uzbekistan, the Tashkent Kidney Transplantation Centre was established in 1972 on the initiative of Academician U.A. Aripov. According to the law of 2017, organs and tissues cannot be the subject of buying and selling; transplantation from close relatives is regulated by a separate regulation. High-technology operations are carried out at the Vohidov Centre, the Republican Scientific Centre of Emergency Medical Care and the Tashkent City Nephrology Hospital. At the basis of any national document lie the principles of non-maleficence, informed voluntary consent and social justice.

t: History of kidney transplantation in Uzbekistan
n: Let us dwell on the history of kidney transplantation in Uzbekistan. The Tashkent Kidney Transplantation Centre was established in 1972 on the initiative of Academician U.A. Aripov; 1970–1973 was the period in which the centre took shape. Initially 6–8 operations a year were performed, and in 1973–1983, 20–25 operations a year; haemodialysis amounted to 3–3.5 thousand procedures a year. In 1994 the Criminal Code was adopted: an organ is retrieved from a cadaver only with the permission of relatives or with lifetime consent, and for this reason kidney transplantation stopped. In 2017 the law "On the transplantation of human tissues and organs" was adopted: an organ cannot be the subject of buying and selling.

t: Procedure for donation by close relatives
n: Let us consider the procedure for donation by close relatives. A close relative may be a donor: parents, brothers, sisters, a spouse, children, including adopted ones, as well as grandparents and grandchildren. A kidney or a portion of the liver may not be taken from persons under 18, persons lacking legal capacity, persons deprived of liberty, pregnant women, and persons with drug addiction or chronic alcoholism. The final decision is made by a special commission established by the Ministry of Health; the donor's written, free and conscious consent is required. After the operation the donor and the recipient remain under the supervision of a preventive dispensary for at least three years.

The third quick question and general review. Who must declare an objection under presumed consent? The person who is against organ retrieval, or his relatives. What is needed to retrieve an organ under presumed dissent? Legally formalised consent; without it the organ cannot be used. Attention: do not confuse these two presumptions. In one, the organ is retrieved if no objection is declared; in the other, consent is mandatory. Recall the dates: Harvard criteria, 1968; World Medical Association declaration, 1987; Islamic Fiqh Academy resolution, 1988.

Let us sum up. Non-maleficence, informed voluntary consent and social justice underlie all transplantation documents. In the United States and Europe about 35 per cent of those in need do not live to receive an operation. Brain death: irreversible loss of consciousness, cessation of spontaneous breathing and loss of brainstem reflexes. The main chain of the topic: 4 types, that is, auto, iso, allo, xeno; donation, living and cadaveric; brain death as the criterion of death; types of presumption; shortage, justice and consent.
